certificationCard.description: Anthropic's architecture-level credential for engineers who design AI systems rather than just build them. The CCAR-F tests your ability to decompose problems into agent workflows, wire up MCP servers that external tools can talk through, configure Claude Code for team-wide consistency, and make the tradeoffs that keep multi-agent pipelines reliable under real production load.

keyConcepts.h2: Claude Certified Architect Foundations: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Designing Multi-Agent Systems
blocks.body: Over a quarter of the exam asks you to architect systems where multiple agents collaborate on a task. You need to decide when a single agent with several tools is enough and when to split work across specialized subagents coordinated by a hub. The exam presents scenarios — a compliance review pipeline, an automated onboarding flow, a research-and-write workflow — and asks which orchestration pattern fits, where failures will surface, and how to add human checkpoints without bottlenecking throughput.

blocks.heading: MCP Servers and Tool Boundaries
blocks.body: The Model Context Protocol gives Claude a standardized way to reach databases, APIs, file systems, and other services. The exam tests your judgment on designing those integrations: what belongs inside one MCP server vs. split across two, when to use stdio transport (local, single-client) vs. SSE (remote, multi-client), how to write tool schemas tight enough that Claude rarely mis-invokes them, and what security controls to put between the model and your production systems.

blocks.heading: Claude Code for Teams and CI/CD
blocks.body: Claude Code is a terminal-based coding agent. The CCAR-F goes beyond using it and into configuring it at the team level. You need to understand how CLAUDE.md files layer — user-level defaults, repo-root project context, directory-level overrides — and how to write custom slash commands, set permission hooks, and plug Claude Code into continuous integration pipelines so it can review pull requests, run migrations, or enforce style guides automatically.

blocks.heading: Prompt Architecture for Complex Applications
blocks.body: At the architect level, prompts are system components, not one-off instructions. The exam tests multi-section system prompts that define roles, constraints, output formats, and escalation rules all in one document. You need to know how to enforce JSON output via tool-use schemas, build few-shot examples that handle edge cases, and design validation-and-retry loops that feed parsing errors back to Claude so it self-corrects. Expect questions on context-window budgeting — how much of the window to reserve for instructions vs. user content vs. tool results.

blocks.heading: Keeping Systems Reliable as They Scale
blocks.body: The final domain covers what goes wrong when an agent runs in production. You need iteration limits that stop runaway loops, circuit breakers that pause work and escalate rather than silently failing, context-management strategies for conversations that approach the window limit, and handoff patterns that pass curated summaries between agents instead of dumping entire histories. The exam also tests graceful degradation — what should happen when a tool is down, a model returns garbage, or context is exhausted.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Claude Certified Architect Foundations Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The CCAR-F rewards system-design instinct more than memorized syntax. If you have designed and operated a production system that uses Claude agents, MCP, or Claude Code at the team level, you are well-positioned. If not, build one first.

blocks.heading: Build a Multi-Agent Workflow End-to-End
blocks.body: Pick a task that naturally decomposes — say, research a topic, draft a report, and fact-check the result — and implement it with a coordinator agent that delegates to subagents. Pay attention to how you pass context between agents, where failures happen, and what metrics you would monitor. That experience directly maps to exam questions.

blocks.heading: Stand Up an MCP Server
blocks.body: Build a server that exposes two or three tools (a database lookup, a file reader, a webhook sender). Connect it to Claude Code or a custom agent. Notice when Claude mis-selects a tool and ask yourself what you would change in the schema to fix it. That debugging habit is what the MCP questions test.

blocks.heading: Configure Claude Code on a Real Codebase
blocks.body: Write CLAUDE.md files at different directory levels and observe how Claude Code merges them. Create a custom slash command, set up a pre-commit hook, and run Claude Code in a CI job. The exam tests the configuration hierarchy and conflict-resolution rules — hands-on experience makes those questions obvious.

blocks.heading: Practice Architectural Tradeoff Conversations
blocks.body: The exam is not about right vs. wrong — it is about better vs. worse given constraints. When you see a question with four plausible answers, ask yourself which option handles the constraint the question emphasized (latency? cost? security? compliance?) without introducing a new failure mode. That lens resolves most ambiguous choices.

blocks.heading: Study Failure Modes, Not Just Happy Paths
blocks.body: What happens when the third tool call in a five-step pipeline fails? What if the model hallucinates a tool name that doesn't exist? What if the context window fills up mid-conversation? The exam loves these edge cases. Catalog five or six failure scenarios and write down the recovery strategy for each.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Certification After Architect Foundations
nextCertsAfter.intro: After earning the Architect Foundations credential, advance to the professional level:

sampleQuestions.question: A legal team needs an agent that reads contracts, flags risky clauses, and drafts suggested revisions. Which orchestration pattern fits best?
options: One agent that reads, flags, and rewrites in a single prompt

A coordinator that sends the contract to a clause-extraction subagent, routes flagged clauses to a risk-assessment subagent, and passes high-risk items to a drafting subagent — with human review before any revision is finalized
Three independent agents that each process the full contract separately and vote on the output
A rule-based system with no AI involvement
sampleQuestions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke orchestration lets each subagent specialize — one excels at extraction, another at risk scoring, another at legal drafting. The coordinator manages sequencing and error handling, and human review before finalization provides accountability for high-stakes legal output.

sampleQuestions.question: An MCP server exposes a tool that executes SQL queries against a production database. What is the most critical architectural safeguard?
options: Using the fastest transport protocol for lower latency
Restricting the tool to read-only queries via a dedicated database role, enforcing parameterized queries to prevent injection, requiring authentication, and logging every query for audit
Caching every query result to reduce database load
Adding a disclaimer in the tool description that says 'be careful'
sampleQuestions.explanation: When an AI agent has database access, defense in depth is mandatory: read-only roles prevent accidental writes, parameterized queries block injection, authentication ensures only authorized agents connect, and audit logs create accountability. A disclaimer in the tool description provides no actual protection.

sampleQuestions.question: A repo has a root-level CLAUDE.md that says 'always use TypeScript strict mode' and a subdirectory CLAUDE.md that says 'JavaScript is acceptable in this folder.' Which instruction does Claude Code follow when editing a file in the subdirectory?
options: The root-level instruction always takes precedence
The directory-level instruction overrides the root for files in that folder, because Claude Code resolves instructions from most-specific to least-specific
Both instructions are ignored in favor of the user-level config
Claude Code prompts the user to resolve the conflict
sampleQuestions.explanation: Claude Code uses a specificity hierarchy: directory-level CLAUDE.md overrides repo-root for files in that directory, just as a .eslintrc in a subdirectory overrides the root config. More specific instructions take precedence over more general ones.

sampleQuestions.question: An agentic loop has made 20 tool calls without completing its task. What is the best architectural response?
options: Let it continue indefinitely — it will eventually finish
Trigger a circuit breaker that pauses the agent, captures its state and the reasoning so far, and either escalates to a human or retries with a narrower task scope
Restart the loop from scratch with the same instructions
Lower the temperature to make the agent more deterministic
sampleQuestions.explanation: Circuit breakers are essential for production agents. Capturing state enables debugging, and escalation or a refined retry prevents repeated failure. Unlimited loops waste tokens and risk cascading errors, while a blind restart discards useful partial progress.

sampleQuestions.question: You are handing off context from a research agent to a writing agent. Which method preserves quality while keeping token costs manageable?
options: Pass the entire raw conversation history from the research agent
Have the research agent produce a structured summary of findings — key facts, sources, and open questions — and pass only that summary plus the writing task instructions to the writing agent
Give the writing agent access to the research agent's tools so it can re-research everything
Store the research output in a database and give the writing agent a SQL tool to query it
sampleQuestions.explanation: Raw conversation histories contain dead ends, tool noise, and irrelevant exploration that bloat the context window. A curated summary gives the writing agent exactly the information it needs, at a fraction of the token cost, and produces more focused output.

sampleQuestions.question: When designing a system prompt for a production application that processes thousands of requests per day, what is the most important structural consideration?
options: Keep the system prompt under 50 tokens for cost savings

Organize the prompt into clearly separated sections — role definition, output format with schema, constraints and guardrails, and escalation rules — so behavior is consistent across all requests and easy to update when requirements change
Write the prompt in casual conversational language to feel more natural
Change the system prompt randomly for each request to increase variety
sampleQuestions.explanation: Production system prompts are infrastructure. Structured sections make behavior predictable across thousands of invocations and allow targeted updates (change the output format without touching the role definition). Unstructured or variable prompts produce inconsistent results at scale.

sampleQuestions.question: An architect needs to choose between stdio and SSE transport for an MCP server. Which scenario clearly favors SSE?
options: A local development tool used by a single developer on their laptop
A shared service running in a cloud container that serves multiple Claude Code instances and external API clients simultaneously
A simple file-reading utility for a CI pipeline
A one-off script that runs once and exits
sampleQuestions.explanation: SSE transport is designed for remote, multi-client deployments. A cloud-hosted service serving multiple concurrent clients needs HTTP-based transport. Stdio is simpler and better for local, single-client scenarios like IDE plugins or CI scripts.

sampleQuestions.question: A customer onboarding pipeline uses Claude to verify documents, check compliance, and generate welcome materials. The compliance check occasionally produces false positives that block legitimate customers. What is the best architectural improvement?
options: Remove the compliance check entirely to improve throughput

Add a confidence score to the compliance agent's output; auto-approve high-confidence passes, auto-reject clear violations, and route borderline cases to a human reviewer with the agent's reasoning attached
Lower the model's temperature to zero so it never flags false positives
Run the compliance check twice and use the more lenient result
sampleQuestions.explanation: A confidence-tiered approach handles the tradeoff between automation speed and accuracy. Clear cases are processed instantly, while uncertain cases get human review. Attaching the agent's reasoning helps the reviewer decide quickly, maintaining throughput without sacrificing compliance quality.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the primary benefit of using Claude Code hooks in a development workflow?
options: Hooks make Claude Code run faster by skipping unnecessary steps
Hooks trigger automated actions — linting, testing, validation — in response to specific Claude Code events, so quality gates run automatically as the agent makes changes
Hooks are required for Claude Code to read files from disk
Hooks let Claude Code bypass code review entirely
sampleQuestions.explanation: Hooks integrate Claude Code into existing development quality standards by attaching automated checks to events like file edits or commits. This ensures AI-generated changes pass the same gates as human changes, without requiring manual intervention.

sampleQuestions.question: A multi-agent system processes insurance claims. The coordinator agent spawns subagents for claim intake, policy lookup, and payout calculation. The policy-lookup subagent occasionally returns stale data because the policy database was recently updated. What architectural change addresses this?
options: Cache all policy data at startup so the subagent never queries the database

Ensure the policy-lookup tool always queries the database at request time rather than relying on cached data, and add a staleness check that compares the record's last-modified timestamp against the claim's submission date
Replace the subagent with a hardcoded lookup table
Run the entire pipeline twice and compare results
sampleQuestions.explanation: Stale data in a claims pipeline creates compliance risk. The fix is architectural: the tool must query live data (not cache), and a staleness check catches edge cases where a policy was updated between claim submission and processing. This is a standard pattern for data-sensitive agent workflows.
